title: What shows the factory's state while you talk to Coordination?
body: Coordination's terminal is the provider's own interactive screen, and Coordination only hears about new events when the daemon can nudge it at a boundary. A long Coordination turn, or time you spend in another agent's terminal, can therefore hide that something is waiting on you. Options: (A) Conversation only. Coordination reports in its turns, and `asmai status` in another shell gives the facts. (B) A one-row AsmAI status line under the provider's screen in every attached terminal, drawn from daemon state: what is waiting on you, the focused job, the running jobs, and any agent whose input you hold. The attach client draws the provider's screen itself, as tmux does, and gives it one row less. (C) The same facts squeezed into the terminal window title, replacing the provider's own title.
try: Setting Q1, any scenario. Step 4 of 'Two jobs, one decision' shows the flag appearing before Coordination can mention it.
rec: B. What is waiting on you comes from the daemon, not from Coordination's paraphrase, so it is right even mid-turn and costs no tokens. It also keeps reminding you that you still hold another agent's input, which matters because detaching without releasing leaves that agent paused. The cost is drawing the provider's screen in the attach client. ADR 0001 already makes terminal emulation AsmAI's job, and both providers' screens must be qualified one row shorter.
options: A: conversation only, plus asmai status
B: daemon status line in every attached terminal
C: terminal window title

title: How do Coordination's automated turns appear while you are talking?
body: Coordination is both your counterpart and the delivery driver. It routes handoffs and reacts to results in the same terminal you are typing in. Already settled: the daemon nudges only at a boundary and never while you have unsent text, and the provider queues anything you send while a turn is running. Options: (A) Full replies: each automated turn reads like a normal Coordination reply. (B) One line per item, tagged with its job number, and a flagged block for anything that needs you; detail on request. (C) Hold routine items while you are attached: only items that need you are delivered, and progress, outcomes and handoffs wait until you leave.
try: Setting Q2, scenario 'Two jobs, one decision'. Under C, watch job 15's handoff stay undelivered in Coordination's inbox.
rec: B. Delivery never waits on whether you are present, and the conversation stays readable. C stalls work between roles for as long as you stay attached, because Coordination cannot route a handoff it has not fetched. That conflicts with continuing independent authorized work.
options: A: full replies
B: one job-tagged line per item; a flagged block when it needs me
C: hold routine items while I am attached

title: How does one conversation keep several jobs apart?
body: One Coordination leader serves every job and loads a job's brief when it switches jobs. Each thing you type needs to belong to a job. Options: (A) A focused job. Your messages apply to it unless you name another job ('14: …' or 'job 14'). 'Switch to 14' moves the focus; Coordination says so and loads that job's brief. A new request opens a new job, which takes the focus. Questions about everything ('what is running?') need no job. (B) Coordination works out the job from each message and asks only when unsure. (C) Every message must start with a job number.
try: Free play: 'Send: switch to 14', then type to Coordination. Each message shows the job it was filed under.
rec: A. It matches the existing rule that a leader loads a job's brief when it switches jobs, it makes a wrong job visible straight away, and it keeps typing light. Every Coordination line about a job carries the job number, including automated lines.
options: A: a focused job with explicit switching
B: Coordination infers the job per message
C: job number required on every message

title: Which decisions can you answer in the terminal, and which only in Lavish?
body: Already settled: reviews and all grilling and Wayfinder questions go through Lavish. Other escalations, such as choosing between two viable approaches or approving a provider replacement, are open. Options: (A) Lavish for every decision request; the terminal only announces it and gives the link. (B) A single-choice escalation may be answered in the terminal; reviews, grilling and Wayfinder questions, and anything with several questions go to Lavish. Each decision version has exactly one answer surface, fixed when it is presented and shown with it. (C) You choose for each request.
try: Setting Q4, scenarios 'Two jobs, one decision' and 'Grilling goes to Lavish'.
rec: B. Under the authority policy, escalations between distinct approaches may be frequent, and a one-line reply keeps them light. With one fixed surface per version, a terminal reply and a Lavish answer can never race each other.
options: A: Lavish for every decision
B: terminal for single choices; Lavish for the rest; one surface per version
C: I choose per request

title: What makes something you said in the conversation count as yours?
body: What you type creates mandates, grants and decision answers, and Coordination is the one interpreting it. Options: (A) Witnessed turns. The daemon journals every message you submit, word for word, in any agent's terminal. Because it owns input, it knows which submissions were yours and which were its own nudges. A record attributed to you (an answer, grant, mandate or scope change) must cite one of your messages, submitted after the decision version it answers was shown. Coordination's reading is stored next to your words, and the owning leader receives both. (B) Coordination's statement is enough, and the daemon checks nothing. (C) Nothing from the conversation counts; every human decision goes through Lavish or an `asmai` command.
try: Setting Q5, scenarios 'Typing while it changes' and 'Things that must fail'.
rec: A. It closes the two real failures the prototype shows: an answer typed against an older version, and an agent attributing words to you that you never typed. Like the agent command guard, this protects against mistakes, not against a hostile process running as you.
options: A: daemon-witnessed messages, cited by every record attributed to me
B: Coordination's word
C: the conversation never records decisions

title: Who collects your Lavish answers?
body: Lavish is where you answer reviews and grilling rounds, and the daemon already supervises the Lavish server. Options: (A) The daemon. It listens on every pending page, journals what you sent word for word as your answer to that decision version, routes it to the owning leader's inbox, and tells Coordination, which confirms in one line. When a decision gets a new version its page is reissued, and answers from the old page are refused. (B) The leader or worker that built the page polls Lavish from inside its own turn. (C) Coordination polls every page.
try: Scenario 'Grilling goes to Lavish', and step 8 of 'Things that must fail'.
rec: A. A blocking poll inside an agent's turn ties that agent up and can lose a round if the turn is interrupted. When the daemon collects answers, a Lavish answer is the same kind of evidence as a witnessed message.
options: A: the daemon collects and routes answers
B: the page's author polls
C: Coordination polls every page

title: What do you see when you come back to the conversation?
body: You run `asmai` after time away, and work kept running. Options: (A) A daemon catch-up. Before the live conversation, the attach client prints what changed since you left, taken from the journal: what is waiting on you (with Lavish links and the forwarding command), jobs that finished, failed or paused, agents waiting in their own terminal, input you still hold, and your saved unsent text. It is one line when nothing changed, and Coordination narrates only if you ask. (B) Coordination writes a welcome-back summary every time you return. (C) Nothing automatic; you ask, or run `asmai status`.
try: Setting Q7, scenario 'Leave and come back'.
rec: A. It is complete, instant and costs no turn. A narrated summary covers only what Coordination has already fetched, and it can be wrong.
options: A: daemon catch-up digest
B: Coordination narrates every return
C: nothing automatic

title: What happens to text you had not sent when you leave the conversation?
body: Two settled rules collide here: detaching returns Coordination to automated delivery immediately, and the daemon never types into the conversation while you have unsent text. Options: (A) Save and clear. The daemon journals the unsent text, clears Coordination's input box at the next boundary and resumes delivery. The catch-up gives the text back for you to copy; it is never retyped automatically. (B) Keep it. The text stays, and nothing reaches Coordination until you return; other roles keep working, but handoffs through Coordination wait. (C) Keep it for a short grace period (for example two minutes, to cover SSH drops), then do A.
try: Setting Q8, scenario 'Leave and come back'.
rec: A. Delivery should not depend on a half-typed sentence, and nothing you typed is lost. Clearing the input box is automated input, so it becomes a qualification case for each provider version.
options: A: save it and clear the input box
B: keep it; Coordination receives nothing until I return
C: keep it for a grace period, then save and clear

title: When you release an agent after intervening, what happens to its work?
body: Already settled: take and release are explicit, automated drafts are recorded and cleared, native prompts are answered in place, and a correction is always a new dispatch. Options: (A) It depends on what you did. If you only answered native prompts, the same dispatch continues. If you typed any message, that dispatch is superseded. The owning leader receives the intervention record (your messages word for word, your prompt answers, cleared drafts, effects recorded meanwhile, and an optional note you give at release) and resumes the worker with a new dispatch after reconciling. Messages held during the intervention are delivered after that. (B) Every intervention waits for the owner to reconcile. (C) Release always resumes the same dispatch, and the owner just receives the record.
try: Setting Q9, scenario 'Step into a worker'. Free play can also release after only answering the prompt.
rec: A. Answering a permission prompt should not stall the worker, but anything you tell it changes its course and has to reach its owner first. C conflicts with the rule in Define work state and coordination contracts that a correction is always a new dispatch.
options: A: prompt answers only, same dispatch; typed messages, owner reconciles and issues a new dispatch
B: owner always reconciles
C: always resume the same dispatch
